name: Apigenin
lead: Apigenin (4',5,7-trihydroxyflavone) is a plant flavone found in parsley, celery, celeriac and especially chamomile, where it makes up about 68 percent of the flavonoids in the flowers [1]. It is sold as a dietary supplement and became popular in sleep-supplement discussion, where it is often paired with magnesium and theanine.

In laboratory work apigenin binds the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors, which is the basis of claims that it calms and aids sleep, although studies disagree on how it interacts with that site [1]. Reviews describe a broad range of preclinical findings, including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and anticancer effects [2][3].

No sources reviewed report a controlled trial showing that apigenin supplements improve sleep or appearance. Human registrations exist for related topics but mostly concern absorption, sperm cryopreservation, sepsis and other conditions [4][5][6].

paras: Apigenin is a yellow crystalline solid with low water solubility that has historically been used to dye wool [1][3]. It is synthesized in plants from phenylalanine via the phenylpropanoid pathway [3]. Dried parsley is among the richest sources, and chamomile flowers contain a high share of apigenin among their flavonoids [1].

In vitro work reports competitive binding to the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors [1]. A widely cited 1998 study also tested phytoestrogens, including apigenin, against estrogen receptor beta [7]. Grokipedia additionally describes inhibition of CD38 and elevation of NAD+, a claim from an AI-generated source [3].

A 2019 review summarized preclinical work on apigenin across cancer, inflammation and neuroprotection and noted the compound's low solubility and bioavailability as obstacles [2]. A 2002 review of flavonoid bioavailability and safety places apigenin within a large class whose absorption in humans is limited [8].

No published trial was found testing apigenin for sleep or looks. Registered human studies include a completed absorption and metabolism study in 17 healthy volunteers [4], a trial of apigenin in elderly sepsis patients [5], and a completed supplement-combination study on stress and sleep (n=115) whose results are not summarized in the sources reviewed [6]. A cardiovascular-risk trial and an apigenin trial for high-risk breast clinic patients (withdrawn) are also registered [9][10].

lore.intro: Apigenin is discussed in sleep-stack conversation as the chamomile compound that helps with falling asleep.

claims.claim: Apigenin before bed improves sleep quality.
claims.believers: Users on sleep-supplement forums say it relaxes them via GABA activity.
claims.experts: Laboratory studies show GABA-A binding, but conflicting findings and no trial results confirm sleep benefits in the sources reviewed [1][6].

claims.claim: Apigenin inhibits CD38 and raises NAD+ for anti-aging.
claims.believers: Proponents cite the mechanism as an anti-aging benefit.
claims.experts: The claim appears in an AI-generated encyclopedia; preclinical reviews do not establish human benefit [2][3].

claims.believers: Some cautious users worry about hormonal effects on masculinity.
claims.experts: A 1998 study tested apigenin among phytoestrogens at estrogen receptor beta [7].

card.summary: Chamomile flavone in sleep stacks; GABA-binding in the lab, no sleep or looks trial found.
card.note: Estrogen-receptor activity has been studied in vitro.

quick.overview:
Apigenin is a flavone from chamomile, parsley and celery sold as a sleep supplement. It is popular in sleep stacks.

Lab studies show GABA receptor binding, but no controlled trial of sleep or appearance outcomes was found.
quick.mechanism: Binds the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors in vitro; other proposed mechanisms include CD38 inhibition.
quick.risks: Safety data in humans are limited; it has been tested at estrogen receptors in vitro. It is sold as a supplement.
